newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: German Economics Minister confident on budget target.
newsitem.headline: German Economics Minister confident on budget target.

text.p: German Economics Minister Guenter Rexrodt said on Friday he was confident Germany would meet its budget target to qualify for European Monetary Union despite an unexpected surge in its unemployment rate to a historic high.

Rexrodt said unemployment could rise again next month, but would start falling from May and was still on track to meet the government's forecast of 4.2 million unemployed on average for calendar 1997.

"We will have a curve that means that we come up to a level we do have now, maybe next month a little bit more, but the same dimension. And starting in May it will come down and the average in 1997 will be 4.2 million people," he told a news conference in Sydney. Rexrodt is on an official visit to Australia.

On Thursday, official figures showed the unemployment rate shot up to 12.2 percent in January, the highest rate since January 1933, from 10.8 percent in December. The number of unemployed bolted to 4.66 million, unleashing a series of protests from opposition politicians and trade unions.

The surprise deterioration also forced economists to question the government's ability to achieve its plan to cut the budget deficit to 2.9 percent of gross domestic product (GDP), given the expected surge in unemployment benefits.
Each additional 100,000 unemployed costs the government four billion to five billion marks ($2.4 billion to $3 billion) and the government is aiming for a 105 billion mark ($63.3 billion) deficit.
Germany must cut its deficit to below three percent of GDP to meet its Maastricht treaty obligations and qualify for the European Monetary Union, so there is little room for slippage.
But Rexrodt said the government did not need to change its budget strategy because its unemployment forecast of 4.2 million on average over 1997 would still be met.

He agreed that achieving the budget target would be difficult, but said the government had the right strategy to deal with its trilemma of cutting the deficit while reducing taxes and paying unemployment benefits.

"I think we see and approach solutions we need in order to balance this trilemma and I'm sure Germany will fulfill the criterias of Maastricht and thereby deliver the preconditions for European Monetary Union starting January 1st 1999," he said.
January's surge in unemployment was partly due to the unusually cold winter, but the problem was largely a structural one, he said.
"We are in a very strong international competition and the high wage, the welfare countries like Germany have to adapt their structure to this changed world," he said.
Germany must push on with its privatisations, deregulations and reforms to taxes, pensions and the labour market, he said.
"There is only one way we must go and that is continuing our reform policy," he said.
"There is no alternative. We must go on in this reform policy and I'm sure we will succeed after a particular time."
Meanwhile, Rexrodt also appeared to welcome the fall in the mark to a new 32-month low against the U.S. dollar just before his news conference.
"I'm not concerned about the price relation between the dollar and the German deutschemark, it's part of the normalisation process. It was over-valued for a long time."
"I tell you as the German Minister of Economics, I can live very well with the price relationship between the dollar and the deutschemark," he said when asked about the fall.
The dollar was quoted at 1.6565 marks in afternoon trade in Tokyo.
